title: MaxSketch: Robust Distinct Counting in Streams via Random Projections
claim: Accuracy stays near-perfect as the number of distinct items grows, and looser tolerance yields robust counts on unseen identities.
layout: single line plot, three colored series, accuracy versus true count k
description: A single wide matplotlib line chart titled 'Counting Accuracy ±50 / ±100 / ±150 (Evaluation Unseen People)'. The x-axis is the true number of unique identities k, from about 100 to 5100. The y-axis is accuracy in percent, from 60 to 100. Three marker-and-line series appear: blue for ±50, orange for ±100 and green for ±150. Green sits at 100% for almost the whole range and dips to about 97–98% near k=4000, 4600 and 5000–5100. Orange also sits at 100% until about k=3600, then fluctuates between 91% and 99%. Blue starts at 100%, becomes noisy, and declines to about 60% at k=5100. A legend is in the lower left and a light grid covers the plot. The eye goes first to the steadily falling blue curve.
caption: MaxSketch counting accuracy on the held-out face identity split, reported at tolerances of $\pm 50$, $\pm 100$, and $\pm 150$ across $k \in \{100, 200, \dots, 5100\}$.
abstract: Estimating the number of distinct elements in a data stream is well understood when repeated elements are identical. In modern settings, however, observations are high-dimensional and noisy, so repeated instances of the same object are only approximately similar -- for example, different images of the same individual may vary significantly at the pixel level. Classical sketches such as HyperLogLog rely on consistent hash values for identical elements and break down in this regime. Recent work on robust distinct counting in general metric spaces achieves $\widetildeÎ(\sqrt{n})$ memory, which is tight in the worst case. We show that substantially improved memory guarantees are possible under geometric structure common in learned representations. We introduce MaxSketch, a simple max-linear sketch built from random Gaussian projections, and prove that it succeeds in estimating the number of distinct latent objects. Concretely, we show that under this assumption $m = \widetilde{O} (\log n / \varepsilon^2)$ random projections (and hence $\widetilde{O} (\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ memory) suffice to recover the true distinct count within a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor. Experiments on image streams confirm that MaxSketch accurately estimates distinct counts and generalizes beyond the training regime. Our results bridge classical streaming algorithms and modern representation learning, showing how geometric structure can fundamentally reduce the complexity of distinct counting.
